title: Nuclear Power
resolution: Resolved: The United States should substantially expand its use of nuclear power.
summary: Nuclear plants make about a fifth of America's electricity with almost no carbon emissions, but new plants have been slow and expensive to build. Should the country build more?

background.p: The United States has the world's largest commercial nuclear fleet: 94 reactors at 54 plants in 2024, with nearly 97 gigawatts of capacity, providing about 19% of the country's electricity, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Natural gas provided about 43% and coal about 16% in 2023; wind, hydropower and solar together about a fifth.

Only a few new reactors have come online since 1996: Watts Bar 2 in Tennessee and two units at Plant Vogtle in Georgia (2023 and 2024). Vogtle's expansion finished years behind schedule and far over its original budget. Twelve reactors have closed since 2013, though federal programs have since supported keeping California's Diablo Canyon open and restarting Michigan's Palisades plant.

Nuclear plants emit almost no carbon dioxide while operating and run most hours of the year. Concerns include building cost and time, the long-term storage of spent fuel (the U.S. has no permanent repository), and the risk of rare but serious accidents such as Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011). Newer designs, including small modular reactors, aim to cut costs, but few have been built.

positions: Supporters say costs fall as builders repeat designs, as other countries have shown, and that small modular reactors can be factory-built.
Critics point to recent U.S. and European projects that ran years late and billions over budget, and note small modular reactors are largely unproven commercially.

terms.def: How much electricity a plant actually produces compared with running at full power all the time. Nuclear plants have very high capacity factors.
Electricity supplied steadily around the clock.
Used reactor fuel, which stays radioactive for a very long time and must be stored safely.
A smaller reactor design meant to be built in factories and shipped to sites.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Nuclear power gives steady, low-carbon electricity at scale, and the country should build more.

args.claim: Nuclear provides large amounts of carbon-free electricity around the clock.
args.warrant: Unlike wind and solar, nuclear doesn't depend on weather, so it can replace fossil-fuel plants that run day and night.
args.evidence: EIA data on nuclear's share of generation and capacity factors; emissions data per unit of electricity from international assessments.
args.response: The negative answers that batteries, transmission lines and a mix of renewables can provide steady power more cheaply and sooner.

args.claim: Measured per unit of energy, nuclear's safety record is strong.
args.warrant: Air pollution from burning fossil fuels harms health continuously, while serious nuclear accidents are rare. Counted per unit of electricity, nuclear causes very few deaths.
args.evidence: Studies of deaths per terawatt-hour across energy sources; health research on air pollution from fossil fuels.
args.response: The negative replies that a single major accident can force evacuations and leave land unusable for decades, a kind of harm averages don't capture.

args.warrant: Data centers, electric vehicles and factories are increasing demand; a reliable source that runs most hours helps keep the grid stable.
args.evidence: EIA and utility forecasts of demand growth; grid operator reliability reports.
args.response: The negative argues new reactors take a decade or more, so they won't meet near-term demand.

args.warrant: First-of-a-kind projects are expensive; repeating standard designs builds skilled crews and supply chains that lower later costs.
args.evidence: Cost histories of reactor programs abroad; analyses of Vogtle lessons learned; Department of Energy reports on advanced reactors.
args.response: The negative replies that the U.S. has repeatedly expected learning to cut costs, and recent projects haven't shown it.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Nuclear is too slow and costly to be the right investment, and its risks are unresolved.

args.claim: New nuclear is expensive and slow.
args.warrant: Money spent on a reactor that takes ten or more years could cut more emissions sooner if spent on cheaper, faster options.
args.evidence: Vogtle 3 and 4 schedule and cost history; cost estimates comparing new nuclear with wind, solar and storage.
args.response: The affirmative answers that cheaper sources aren't steady, and storage at grid scale adds large costs of its own.

args.warrant: Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years, and the U.S. still has no permanent repository, so waste piles up at plant sites.
args.evidence: Department of Energy and Government Accountability Office reports on spent fuel storage; the history of the Yucca Mountain project.
args.response: The affirmative replies that spent fuel is small in volume, stored safely in dry casks, and that the barrier is political, not technical.

args.claim: Rare accidents can be very costly.
args.warrant: A serious accident can force evacuations, contaminate land and cost hundreds of billions, a risk that grows with more reactors.
args.evidence: Reports on Fukushima's evacuation and cleanup; Nuclear Regulatory Commission risk assessments.
args.response: The affirmative argues modern designs are safer, and that fossil-fuel pollution causes far more harm every year.

args.warrant: More reactors mean more fuel to protect and more sites that need security, and some fuel supply has depended on imports from countries such as Russia.
args.evidence: Reports on enriched uranium imports; NRC security requirements; international nonproliferation analyses.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the U.S. can expand domestic enrichment, and plants are among the most secure civilian sites.

strawmen.strawman: Nuclear supporters don't care about accidents.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue that per unit of energy nuclear's safety record is strong compared with fossil fuels.
strawmen.steelman: Nuclear produces large amounts of steady, low-carbon power, and measured per unit of electricity its health toll is very low.

strawmen.strawman: Nuclear opponents are just afraid of anything new.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to cost, construction time and the unresolved waste question.
strawmen.steelman: New reactors take a decade and cost far more than planned, and the same money may cut emissions faster elsewhere while waste storage remains unsolved.

weak.why: No energy source is completely safe; claim what the evidence supports.

weak.arg: A nuclear plant could explode like an atomic bomb.
weak.why: Reactor fuel can't explode like a nuclear weapon. Accidents are serious, but this is false and costs credibility.

aff: How long did Vogtle 3 and 4 take to build, and at what cost?
Where would the spent fuel go?
How would expansion meet demand in the next five years?
neg: What would replace nuclear plants at night when there's no sun or wind?
How many deaths per unit of energy does nuclear cause compared with coal?
